transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (Psi CISO), Eli Zhao (Psi Cloud Architect), Ben Carter (Psi SecOps), Anika Patel (Psi Legal)
Shared artifacts: Redwood BYOK runbook (link), HSM connector sketch (link), SOC2 snapshot (redacted)

Summary:
Quick security/compliance review focused on encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK and HSM integration options, audit log retention, and RBAC/SSO requirements. Customer has strict data residency needs for EU/UK; wants BYOK with HSM-backed keys and no vendor escrow. They requested detailed runbook and a benchmark to quantify perf and cost delta with HSM.

Topics:
- Encryption at rest: disk vs object vs model weights
- TLS and mutual auth for in-transit traffic
- KMS options: Redwood-managed, BYOK via cloud KMS, HSM on-prem connector
- Key lifecycle, rotation, and escrow policy
- RBAC / SSO / audit logs for tenant separation
- Residency + replication fallback policies

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we'll do a quick run-through of the encryption runbook and then, Priya, you'll take the HSM slides and the connector notes. Sound good?
[00:12] Marta Lopez: Yep, sounds good. We're mostly here to validate we can meet our compliance bar — SOC2, ISO, and also the internal legal ask around key custody.
[00:20] Eli Zhao: And data residency — we need EU and UK data never to leave region except for backups we control.
[00:25] Jordan Kim: Understood. I'll flag upfront: Redwood supports hosted and private deployments; for BYOK we have a couple patterns — cloud KMS BYOK where you upload a key envelope, or HSM-backed keys where your HSM issues keys and we never see plaintext.
[00:40] Ben Carter: Quick Q — how does that work with model weights? Are those encrypted with the same keys as user data?
[00:48] Priya Shah: Good question. Typically we separate keys: model artifacts are encrypted at rest using a service-level key but we can layer customer-specific encryption (envelope encryption) so you can BYOK-wrap the model keys. There's sometimes a perf lift; we'll show numbers.
[01:10] Eli Zhao: When you say "we can BYOK-wrap the model keys" — does Redwood store any copy of the unwrapped key? We need assurance for non-escrow.
[01:20] Liam Ortiz: Short answer: no. In the HSM pattern, key material never leaves your HSM. For cloud-KMS BYOK the key material is in your KMS; we store only the key identifier and an envelope-wrapped data key.
[01:35] Marta Lopez: I want that in writing — legal will need a clause saying Redwood does not escrow keys or retain unwrapped key material.
[01:42] Jordan Kim: Absolutely, we'll add a section to the runbook and to the contract redline.
[01:47] Anika Patel: And what about key rotation — does rotation force a re-encrypt of all stored model shards or is it a re-envelope operation?
[01:56] Priya Shah: We use envelope encryption. Rotation typically involves generating a new data key and re-wrapping the envelope key — so no full re-encrypt of objects in most cases. There are corner cases for model checkpointing where re-keying is needed, we'll document those.
[02:20] Ben Carter: What about audit trails? We need immutable logs that show key usage — which principal made the call, the KMS key id, timestamps. Retention 7 years.
[02:33] Jordan Kim: Redwood emits detailed audit logs for key operations and model-access-level events; logs can be routed to your SIEM or to a customer-owned log bucket. Retention policy is configurable — 7 years is long but possible if you manage storage; we can also support tiered archival.
[02:50] Eli Zhao: Who signs the TLS certs between Redwood runtime and storage? We want mTLS with client certs from our PKI.
[02:59] Priya Shah: We support mutual TLS; you can push client certs and our fleet will validate against your CA. For hosted customers we can also federate with your internal PKI via an intermediary. There's a short latency impact at handshake but negligible for steady-state.
[03:18] Jordan Kim: Note: sometimes transcription says "m T L S" — it's mTLS. Also "KV cache" often comes out as "KV cash" in the auto transcript.
[03:24] Marta Lopez: (laughs) noted.
[03:26] [04:00] Priya Shah: I'll pull up the HSM connector slide. The two main modes: 1) HSM-on-prem bridge where a connector in your VPC talks to your HSM over a secure channel; 2) HSM-as-a-service where a customer-managed HSM in cloud with strict tenant isolation issues keys via an HSM-bridging API.
[04:22] Eli Zhao: For mode 1, does the connector require inbound ports opened? We try to avoid inbound rules on our HSM.
[04:30] Priya Shah: No inbound. Connector is outbound from your VPC to Redwood control plane, and then TLS to the HSM endpoint; everything is authenticated. We use client certs and token-based auth.
[04:45] Ben Carter: And for the HSM vendor — do you have a list of supported modules? We use Thales at present.
[04:51] Liam Ortiz: We support common HSMs including Thales nShield, AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and Safenet. For other vendors we can do a certification pass.
[05:05] Marta Lopez: Can you explain the BYOK envelope flow end-to-end — like, request flow when an inference request comes in that needs decryption for a model shard?
[05:15] Priya Shah: Sure. Inference request arrives -> runtime checks tenant policy -> retrieves encrypted model shard key envelope from object store metadata -> calls KMS (your KMS or our HSM bridge) to unwrap the data key -> runtime decrypts shard in memory or uses streaming decrypt path -> continues. We keep the unwrapped key only in memory and evict it from the KV cache after a TTL.
[05:36] Eli Zhao: That ttl — what's the default? Can we force zero-reuse?
[05:41] Priya Shah: Default is 5 minutes for throughput reasons, but you can set zero-reuse for stricter controls at cost of latency. We'll put recommended profiles in the runbook.
[05:55] Anika Patel: On legal: what's Redwood's stance on escrow? We have procurement saying no escrow but want continuity guarantees.
[06:03] Jordan Kim: We provide an SLA and can offer cross-region replication options that keep encrypted backups in your control. For continuity, we can do an emergency key release process under mutually-agreed legal conditions, but we can also support NO-ESCROW where keys are fully customer-controlled and continuity is customer's responsibility.
[06:22] Marta Lopez: Hmm, we'll need that emergency path described with legal triggers.
[06:27] Jordan Kim: We'll draft language.
[06:29] [06:40] Ben Carter: Regarding logs again, is the audit log tamper-evident? We prefer signed append-only logs.
[06:47] Priya Shah: We can provide signed event bundles using a signing key, with hash chaining for append-only proof. The logs can be exported to your immutable archival. There's a small compute overhead for signing.
[07:05] Eli Zhao: On residency: we will not allow key material to be imported into non-EU regions. How do you handle failover? If a compute host in US needs to serve a EU customer, what's the fallback?
[07:18] Jordan Kim: Policy-based routing — requests for EU-tenanted data are routed to EU-only pools. If EU capacity is exhausted, the policy can either queue, fail open to a lower-security model, or fail closed. We typically recommend queuing or fail closed for regulated data. We'll show config examples.
[07:37] Marta Lopez: Can you do a short demo of the console RBAC? We need role separation between devs and security ops, and we use SAML SSO.
[07:45] Liam Ortiz: Sure, quick walk-through — we have role templates: Viewer, Operator, Key Custodian, Admin. Key Custodian has rights to import/wrap keys but not to spin up public endpoints. We integrate with SAML and SCIM for user provisioning.
[08:05] Ben Carter: Does Key Custodian need to be a human? We want to integrate with our service account model.
[08:11] Priya Shah: Service accounts are supported; you can issue time-limited tokens tied to your IdP.
[08:18] Eli Zhao: About performance — you mentioned a perf delta. Can you ballpark HSM-on-path latency per unwrap?
[08:25] Priya Shah: Typical HSM unwrap ~ 20-50ms depending on network and HSM model. For high QPS we do caching of unwrapped data keys with strict TTLs to avoid per-request unwrap. We'll quantify in the benchmark.
[08:40] Jordan Kim: Note — that 20-50ms is just the unwrap op; the total per-token cost will depend on batching, sequence lengths, and model.
[08:48] Marta Lopez: Are there scenarios where we can't avoid sending data to Redwood-managed storage even if we BYOK? For example, model telemetry or embeddings?
[08:58] Jordan Kim: Telemetry can be configured to send to your log sinks; we can also redact or not collect embeddings for customer-specified datasets. For hosted we've got a policy to minimize PII collection.
[09:12] Anika Patel: We need the SOC2 and ISO documentation — do you publish certs?
[09:18] Jordan Kim: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 summaries; we'll share the certs and a redacted SOC2 report.
[09:26] Eli Zhao: Any interaction with our HSM vendor for audits? They may ask to see connectors.
[09:31] Liam Ortiz: We can provide connector manifests and perform joint testing; we can also do an on-site review if required.
[09:40] Ben Carter: Do you support bring-your-own-hsm (BYOH) for cloud HSMs — like CloudHSM with customer root?
[09:47] Priya Shah: Yes, you can configure a customer-managed KMS cluster in the cloud and provide the key policy so Redwood's runtime can call that KMS. Keys never leave the customer's KMS.
[09:58] Marta Lopez: How do you handle backup encryption? Backups go to object storage — are those encrypted with the same envelope keys?
[10:05] Priya Shah: Backups are encrypted with envelope keys; you can choose to have a separate backup key. We recommend separate key policies for backups with different rotation windows.
[10:18] Eli Zhao: Any risk of side-channel leaks when decrypting model weights in memory?
[10:23] Priya Shah: We follow memory-hard and constant-time primitives where possible; largest risk vectors are within model inference kernels. We minimize in-memory dwell time and zeroize memory after use. For very strict workloads we recommend private deployment so you control the entire host.
[10:42] Jordan Kim: Ok, let's step through an example onboarding flow — Jordan: outline steps 1..7.
[10:50] Jordan Kim: Step 1: sign NDA/holdback agreement. Step 2: define residency and key policy. Step 3: choose HSM pattern (cloud-kms vs on-prem HSM bridge). Step 4: import or generate keys and verify policy. Step 5: run baseline perf tests. Step 6: pilot traffic and monitor audit logs. Step 7: roll to prod.
[11:10] Marta Lopez: How long does a pilot take typically?
[11:12] Priya Shah: 2-6 weeks depending on compliance gating; perf tests + legal review take most of that.
[11:20] Ben Carter: For the pilot we want a non-prod instance in our VPC with HSM bridge. Can you provide Terraform examples?
[11:26] Liam Ortiz: Yes, we'll share Terraform + Ansible snippets in the runbook.
[11:31] Eli Zhao: Regarding cost — if we enable HSM unwrap on every inference, what's the expected monthly cost bump?
[11:38] Priya Shah: It depends heavily on QPS and unwrap frequency; naive per-unwrap cost would be small but at scale adds up. With caching it tends to be a low single-digit percent CPU/infra bump; we'll provide a model with examples.
[11:55] [12:05] Jordan Kim: We're approaching the final part — questions and recap.
[12:09] Marta Lopez: Two final asks: 1) Written assurance of no key escrow; 2) Emergency key release policy with legal triggers.
[12:17] Jordan Kim: We'll draft both and include in the runbook and contract.
[12:20] Eli Zhao: And the benchmark — we want perf numbers for a 13B model with 2k context, comparing cloud-kms unwrap with HSM and with zero-reuse TTL.
[12:31] Priya Shah: Noted — Priya will run that.
[12:34] Ben Carter: Please include measurement of added latency percent and cost per million requests.
[12:38] Priya Shah: Yep.
[12:40] Jordan Kim: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the runbook, connector diagram, Terraform snippets, and the SOC2 artefacts.
[12:50] Marta Lopez: Thanks.
[12:52] Anika Patel: Thanks all.

Recap (auto):
- Redwood supports BYOK via cloud KMS or HSM bridge; keys never stored unwrapped in Redwood control plane for HSM pattern.
- Envelope encryption used for model artifacts; re-wrapping vs full re-encrypt documented.
- mTLS, signed/tamper-evident logs, SCIM/SAML RBAC supported.
- Residency routing policy to prevent cross-region key usage; emergency release is an option with legal triggers.

References shared:
- BYOK onboarding runbook: https://redwood.example/runbooks/byok-onboarding.pdf
- HSM connector sketch: https://redwood.example/artifacts/hsm-connector-v1.png
- SOC2 snapshot (redacted): https://redwood.example/compliance/soc2-2025-redacted.pdf

End of transcript.
